newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African bunker problems highlight growing pains.
newsitem.headline: S.African bunker problems highlight growing pains.

text.p: South Africa's marine bunker fuel market has been plagued by refinery problems this year, highlighting the growing pains of a sector emerging from years of stagnation, industry officials said on Monday.
The current bugbear is Engen Ltd which ran into problems at its Durban refinery bunker unit at the end of August, and is still out of the market.
Engen's difficulties come after a scheduled shutdown at the Caltex -- a Texaco Inc -Chevron Corp venture -- unit in Cape Town, which was followed by technical problems.
"A good five months of this year has seen very tight availability with prices all over the place," one trader said.
Another added, "There is no spare capacity and there is no room for any refinery to go down."
Industry analysts noted South Africa's plentiful supply of cheap coal, plus the apartheid era oil embargo, had pushed it heavily towards coal with little demand for fuel oil.
What fuel oil is produced is sold to the bunker market.
Under sanctions, bunker demand was thin. But the opening up of the economy after the first democratic elections in 1994 has triggered rapid growth.
Bunker fuel sales jumped 27 percent in Durban alone in 1995. Nationwide, total demand last year was about three million tonnes, earning the country some $250 million.
Fortunately, the last two years growth in demand has been matched by refinery expansions, mainly to meet growing demand for higher value products such as gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.
But now that expansion programme has stopped, and the growing bunker market is feeling the pinch.
Several oil companies have said they are considering further expansion in the long term -- but not just yet.
"No one can justify expansion just to meet the demand for bunker fuel," said one industry official.
The oil firms say the series of technical problems this year are unfortunate but that all commitments are being met.

Engen itself has said that it would be able to meet its commitments from reserves until September 20, when it would arrange short-term accommodation agreements with the Royal Dutch/Shell Group /British Petroleum Co Plc (BP) Sapref refinery in Durban.
Traders, however, report that there are at least 12 vessels in South African waters which can only access very small amounts of bunker fuel.
"This adds to South Africa's perceived reputation for not being able to guarantee reliability of supply," said one trader.
The oil companies are not expected to make any definitive decisions on refinery expansion until there is greater clarity on government policy for the tightly controlled oil industry.
The new Minerals and Energy Affairs Minister Penuell Maduna is said to be reviewing options, especially on deregulation, as he settles into office.
The policy review might be more urgently needed than the bunker market alone indicates. Demand for jet fuel has also soared and some sources foresee supply problems building up there too.
"We are seeing the pains of growth in a market that has previously stagnated," one industry source said.
